title: Teachers Cannot Design Around AI Cheating
author: Andrew Barron
summary: Andrew Barron argues that the popular advice to "design around AI" is wrong and at least a year out of date. He starts from survey evidence that many teens regard AI cheating as routine and from familiar symptoms such as a 100% homework average beside a 40% quiz average. His central claim is that assessment has two purposes, measurement and feedback, and that most proposed redesigns (BookTok videos, podcasts, minimal grading, multimodal portfolios) protect neither, since a model can produce the content and the product no longer tells a teacher what a single student knows. He also takes apart a 2025 German study on error-correction exams, saying newer models have already made its conclusion obsolete. His answer is older and more labour-intensive: ongoing formative assessment where teachers watch students think, work and respond in real time, because learning rests on a relationship between teacher and student mediated by content.
points: Assessment exists to measure a defined skill (validity) and to give feedback; any redesign that preserves neither has failed, even if it deters AI.
Fun, low-rigor projects were already weak assessments, and AI has exposed that rather than created it.
Complexity does not AI-proof a task, and skipping to complex tasks bypasses the basic skills that assessment should be sampling.
Assessments should span a continuum of skills so a teacher can locate the point where a student's understanding breaks down.
The durable answer is direct observation: drafts, works in progress and repeated in-class evidence of thinking.
quotes: Assessments have two purposes—measurement and feedback—both of which are challenged by the capabilities of AI.
Measurement requires that what the teacher thinks is being measured is the skill or concept itself, not some confounded version of it. This is validity.

These suggestions mostly undermine the dual purposes of assessment rather than strengthen them, and none of them solves the problem of AI cheating. They largely just ignore the problem and hope that “minimal grading” will entice students to submit their own work.

LLMs can now handle complex assessments and manufacture personal connections or reflections a human might be asked to include to verify authenticity. Plug in any assignment you want, and you will get a plausible answer.
As long as the advice is to somehow outstrip AI’s capabilities through creative design, teachers will be on the losing side of that race.
Skills in all subjects build. The idea that we can AI-proof assessments by making them complex ignores this principle and skips right to the final stages without assessing the basic skills.
The real answer has always been that teachers need to see students thinking, working, discussing, and responding in real time.

Assessment will have to rely on relationships in which teachers directly observe the development of skills in students. All of our attempts to move away from this labor-intensive model will eventually break.
